doc.title: Ray Shiner interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 11, 1998

title: Dispute with a classical conductor on West Side Story dances
summary: A conductor mis-explained jazz eighths at a New York Philharmonic Bernstein birthday piece; Shiner and Walter Rosenberger recorded it in two takes.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: Did you ever have any difficult experiences with classical conductors?
Oh yeah, many.
Well name some. They’re probably gone now.

I had one, which I quoted, it was written up in the Rochester jazz paper, where they did dances from “West Side Story,” which I premiered with the New York Philharmonic in New York. And the conductor, it was a birthday present for Lenny Bernstein. I won’t name the conductor, but he stopped and he explained to me what jazz was. He’s telling me what jazz was, and he’s counting off twelve-eight time, which is the way symphony musicians play dotted eighth and sixteenths.
Oh, right, oh I see.

You know [scats]. They play it like that, and I go [scats] which is the way you’re supposed to play it. So after about three tries and encouragement from the guys in the orchestra — I was going to say guys in the band — the guys in the New York Philharmonic, friends of mine, they said, “Give it to him Ray, don’t take that from him.” Of course that set me off because I said I don’t need this from him. I said, “You want it the way it’s written? The way you’re singing it? Or the way it should be played?”
All right.

So that kind of stopped the conversation. And the guy accompanying me on that bit was the marimba player, who was an original member of the Sauter-Finegan band, Walter Rosenberger. So Walter played the marimba and I played the alto sax and that was it. Bernstein came in a month later to record it. And he just said, “Is my sax player here?” And I says, “Yeah, right here.” “Is my trumpet player here?” And Gino says, “He’s here.” So we were the two outside men from the New York Philharmonic.
Okay. There you go.
So we did two fast takes, and nobody said a word. I don’t know if that explains it.
Yeah, sure it does.
It takes up time. © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

It’s interesting the way you described the way classical musicians think of the swing eighth rhythm too, with the twelve-eight thing. They think of it as a triplet with the first note longer and the second note shorter.
Yeah. Which is wrong.
Which is wrong. But it’s as close as — they need to try to put it in a context that they can understand it. So it’s as close as they can get it I guess. So you did the [scats].
That’s right. That’s at the beginning of the piece.
Right.
Well anyway.
Neat. No I like that story.
It’s part of my life. I played alto sax with the Rochester Philharmonic, the Chicago Orchestra, the New York Philharmonic, I’m a sax player.
